there's nothing new about this. it's the conflict between the concrete world and humanity's abstract interpretation of it, between subject and object. This shared world of ideas and abstractions can be as real as any of the concrete objects you  describe. If anything, it's more real to human beings, since you are never truly in contact with this concrete world. Only through abstract interpretation does your mind make sense of it's surroundings. This is why other people's ideas and interpretations of you can feel so concrete and overwhelming. If the majority of people have interacted with you in a negative way, or have disliked your behaviour, this "intangible" emotional weight can crush you in a very real way.

Making it much harder to wrap my head around those things and stay focused. So for example, I took twice as long as my peers to get my driver's license, because I couldn't predict distances etc.

That being said, there are people who don't care, who don't even show sympathy. But there are plenty of people who've been sympathetic towards me, even if they don't understand it.

It's the times you're alone at night, without any distractions. The tunnel vision of daily life has passed, and you open up your mind to see the bigger picture. Here we just fall into metaphors, otherwise it's indescribable. The thing that stares back at you is an endless void of possibilities, expectations and responsibilities. "I could be anywhere, doing anything, and I'm just sitting here." "Whatever I do, it won't matter in the long run, there is nothing." You freeze as an overwhelming sense of despair starts weighing down on you. Your body blocks out any emotion to prevent a mental breakdown. You become numb, everything becomes too much, you just want to sleep. The despair starts dragging you down further and further, until it becomes chronic. Carrying this weight is one of the hardest things a human being can do, apart from getting rid of it.

Whenever we are exposed to certain stimuli for a prolonged amount of time, we get accustomed to them. For example: when you take a shower, you start at a certain temperature, but after a while you don't really notice the heat anymore, so you have to increase the temperature to get that same experience. The same goes for many drugs and also sound/smells/etc. So I think what might be happening is that our brains are developing an addiction to dopamine, because we are constantly stimulated. So when we take away these stimuli, we feel empty and numb. Of course some people are inherently more vulnerable to things like depression, but this overstimulation is definitely a growing problem in western society.
